title: Why Perimenopause Is the Health Cliff Women Are Not Prepared For
excerpt: One in three women over 35 are unsure whether they have entered perimenopause, a new study finds, as Indian women face earlier menopause and decades of post-menopausal life with little clinical guidance.
body:
• A study of 7,600 U.S. women published in Menopause found that 34% were unsure of their reproductive stage, with uncertainty peaking at 42% among women ages 40–44.
  • Indian women enter menopause at an average age of 46 — five years earlier than the global average of 51 — and will spend 25 to 30 years in a post-menopausal state.
  • Perimenopause, not menopause itself, is increasingly recognized as the critical metabolic window where cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and bone loss risk are set.
  • India's first independent menopause care clinic opened in Mumbai in late 2025, part of a growing movement to break decades of silence around hormonal health.

The Knowledge Gap

A new study published in the journal Menopause by The Menopause Society found that one in three U.S. women over 35 are unsure whether they have entered perimenopause — the hormonal transition that precedes the end of menstruation. Among women ages 40 to 44, the uncertainty rate climbed to 42%.

The study of more than 7,600 women identified three main drivers: symptom confusion (56% of responses), knowledge gaps (28%), and barriers to clinical confirmation and care (16%). Younger women were more likely to cite a lack of information, while those in the 40–44 group more often reported dismissive healthcare encounters.

"Symptom confusion, misconceptions and barriers to care are leaving many women without the clarity and support they need during the menopause transition."

— Dr. Stephanie Faubion, Medical Director, The Menopause Society

No laboratory test or biomarker can definitively confirm perimenopause. Its symptoms — hot flashes, mood swings, irregular cycles, sleep disruption, brain fog — overlap with conditions ranging from thyroid disease to depression, making clinical recognition difficult.

Why Indian Women Face a Steeper Cliff

In India, the stakes are higher. Indian women enter menopause at an average age of 46, five years earlier than the global average of around 51, according to Livemint. With life expectancy now at 70.3 years — a gain of more than 20 years over the last half-century — the majority of Indian women will spend 25 to 30 years in a post-menopausal state.

"Indian women are menopausing earlier, and what I find in women who are coming for consultations is that there is a sense of frustration about not being heard," said Dr. Sukhpreet Patel, a Mumbai gynaecologist who opened India's first independent menopause care clinic at Nana Chowk in December 2025 after building a following of millions on Instagram through her handle @menopausewize.

Premature ovarian failure — when ovaries stop functioning before age 40 — is also rising. Dr. Amarja Paranjpe of Apollo Spectra Mumbai told BW Wellbeing World that in recent months, two out of every ten women visiting her practice showed signs of early menopause, driven by chronic stress, poor nutrition, and sedentary lifestyles.

The Metabolic Inflection Point

Researchers increasingly point to perimenopause, not menopause itself, as the critical window for metabolic and cardiovascular risk. The loss of estrogen during this phase can trigger insulin resistance, accelerate bone density loss, and raise cardiovascular disease risk within months, according to Dr. Mayoni Gooneratne, a former NHS surgeon and founder of Human Health in London.

A study presented at HCPLive found that a carbohydrate-reduction intervention in menopausal women drove BMI from 33.84 to 30.7 and HbA1c from 7.24% to 6.56% over 12 months — results that directly contradicted the assumption that metabolic decline during menopause is inevitable. "This is a strategic opportunity to interfere — it's a pathway to transition rather than decline," said researcher Shaminie Athinarayanan.

Perimenopause typically begins in the early to mid-40s and lasts four to eight years. During this phase, estrogen and progesterone do not decline steadily — they fluctuate unpredictably, which is why symptoms can be severe and confusing long before periods actually stop.

Breaking the Silence

India's menopause conversation has shifted visibly over the past year. Menopausal Mates, started by Mumbai reflexologist Rachel Kurien in 2022, has grown into one of the country's largest support communities. Femtech startups like Miror and Elda Health are building clinical platforms, though the sector remains loss-making. Miror founder Sanjith Shetty has invested more than Rs 5 crore over five years and projects profitability is still five to ten years away.

"For far too long, society has celebrated a woman only for her pregnancy, but ignored her prime phase — perimenopause and menopause," said Shaili Chopra, who organized India's first menopause and midlife wellness festival, Fabulous Over Forty, in Mumbai in mid-2025.

What Women Can Do Now

Experts recommend strength training to counter bone and muscle loss, calcium-rich diets, adequate sleep, and stress management through yoga or meditation. Menopause Hormone Therapy has gained traction globally and in India, though many gynaecologists remain hesitant to prescribe it. Dr. Patel believes attitudes will shift within a decade as evidence and awareness grow. For now, doctors say the most important step is recognition — understanding that perimenopause symptoms are treatable, not something women must simply endure.
image_caption: Perimenopause can begin years before menopause, bringing hormonal shifts that affect bone density, cardiovascular health, and metabolism.
nri_angle: Indian diaspora women face earlier menopause than global averages and often lack culturally sensitive clinical guidance in their adopted countries, making awareness of perimenopause symptoms and treatment options especially critical.
